method: OPEN AND QUOTED from Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome' (2025). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at PMC JATS XML <license> element for PMC12483350 (NCBI efetch; Europe PMC returned 503)). Source text: NCBI efetch JATS XML (Europe PMC fullTextXML returned HTTP 503 on 2026-09-23).

claims.claim: **FCS is a rare recessive disorder** (about 1 to 10 per million) caused by biallelic variants affecting lipoprotein lipase (LPL). It carries a high risk of recurrent, life-threatening acute pancreatitis.
claims.source_text: FCS is an autosomal recessive disorder that affects approximately 1 to 10 individuals per million and is caused by biallelic pathogenic (P) or likely pathogenic (LP) variants in the genes encoding the lipoprotein lipase (LPL) enzyme. In addition to its heterogeneous clinical presentation, FCS is characterized by a greater risk of life-threatening, recurrent acute pancreatitis and type 3 diabetes
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnosis starts with finding severe hypertriglyceridaemia.** Some patients have few or no symptoms. Triglycerides are extremely and persistently high (above 885 mg/dL).
claims.source_text: While some patients present with mild or no symptoms, the diagnostic process begins with the detection of severe hypertriglyceridemia (HTG). … The diagnosis of FCS is largely based on the identification of extreme and persistent elevations in plasma or serum levels of TGs (>885 mg/dL)
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A poor response to standard lipid-lowering drugs is typical,** and FCS is widely underdiagnosed, which delays proper treatment.
claims.source_text: A poor response to conventional lipid-lowering therapies is common among these patients because of impaired lipid clearance. However, FCS remains largely underdiagnosed, which may lead to delayed initiation of adequate treatment
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use a clinical score** to support the diagnosis and to separate FCS from multifactorial chylomicronaemia (MCS). (100% agreement)
claims.source_text: the expert panel recommends the use of clinical scores for the diagnosis of FCS. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). … Available pragmatic scores for the diagnosis of FCS, which rely mainly on clinical parameters (Tables 1 and 2), may assist in differentiating between FCS and multifactorial chylomicronemia syndrome (MCS)
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Features that point to FCS:** no secondary cause of severe hypertriglyceridaemia; past pancreatitis; no response to standard treatment; recurrent unexplained abdominal pain; onset in childhood, adolescence or young adulthood.
claims.source_text: [3.1] Absence of secondary factors for severe HTG. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.2] History of pancreatitis. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.3] Refractoriness to conventional treatments for HTG. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.4] A history of unexplained recurrent abdominal pain due to other reasons. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [3.5] Early disease onset (childhood, adolescence, or young adulthood).
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Typical lipid profile:** normal or low LDL cholesterol, low HDL cholesterol, a triglyceride-to-total-cholesterol ratio above 5, and low-to-normal apoB. Diabetes appearing after the lipid diagnosis also fits (75% agreement).
claims.source_text: [3.6] Consistent lipid profile (normal or low levels of direct low-density lipoprotein cholesterol [LDL-C], low levels of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol [HDL-C], TG/total cholesterol (TC) ratio >5, and low-to-normal levels of apolipoprotein B [apoB]). … [3.7] Onset of diabetes following the diagnosis of HTG. Expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 75%).
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Body weight does not rule it out:** a normal BMI may be a clue, but FCS occurs in normal-weight and overweight people.
claims.source_text: a normal body mass index (BMI) might serve as a useful indicator; however, both normal-weight and overweight individuals can develop FCS
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genes to test first:** LPL, GPIHBP1 and APOA5, then APOC2 and LMF1. LPL variants explain 50–90% of cases, depending on the population.
claims.source_text: [4.1] LPL. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [4.2] GPIHBP1. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [4.3] APOA5. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 83.3%). [4.4] APOC2. Expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 75%). [4.5] LMF1. … Depending on the target population, 50-90% of patients with FCS may have biallelic variants in the LPL gene
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Genetic testing is the preferred way to confirm FCS.** Where it is not available, clinical assessment including scores is the best practical method.
claims.source_text: under ideal circumstances, genetic testing is the recommended method to confirm the diagnosis of FCS. … under real-world circumstances, the clinical evaluation of the patient (including clinical scores) is the best diagnostic method for FCS.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A negative genetic test does not exclude FCS:** nearly 25% of patients with a typical picture test negative.
claims.source_text: nearly 25% of patients presenting with clinical features consistent with FCS have a negative genetic test result
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **If genetics are negative or show a variant of unknown significance, measure LPL activity** where available. Anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies or whole-exome sequencing are alternatives. Each laboratory sets its own cut-off; activity in FCS is usually 25% or less.
claims.source_text: the LPL activity assay (if available) should be conducted in patients with clinical features and laboratory findings consistent with FCS + a negative genetic test or a variant of unknown significance (VUS). … this preferential recommendation does not preclude the use of other strategies, such as the identification of anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies or whole-exome sequencing. … Each laboratory should set their own cutoff values to measure LPL activity, which is typically ≤25% of said value among patients with FCS
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **A single heterozygous variant counts as a negative result,** as does a variant of unknown significance in these genes.
claims.source_text: the presence of heterozygous P/LP variants in a single canonical gene or the detection of homozygous or heterozygous VUS in the same genes are also regarded as negative genetic test results.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Definite FCS:** clinical, biochemical and genetic findings fit, and LPL activity is absent. **MCS:** findings fit but genetics are negative and LPL activity is normal.
claims.source_text: [14.1] Clinical, biochemical, and genetic testing consistent with FCS and absent LPL activity: diagnosis of FCS. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 100%). [14.2] Clinical and biochemical traits consistent with FCS + negative genetic testing + normal LPL activity: diagnosis of MCS.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Possible FCS:** negative genetics with low LPL activity. **Probable FCS:** inconclusive genetics with low LPL activity. Inconclusive genetics with normal LPL activity suggests MCS.
claims.source_text: the possible diagnosis of FCS should be considered in patients with clinical and biochemical features consistent with FCS + negative genetic tests + low LPL activity. … the probable diagnosis of FCS should be considered in patients with clinical and biochemical traits consistent with FCS + inconclusive genetic tests + low LPL … the diagnosis of MCS should be considered in patients with clinical and biochemical traits consistent with FCS + inconclusive genetic tests + normal LPL
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Think of autoimmune chylomicronaemia (anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies)** when hypertriglyceridaemia is intermittent, genetics are inconclusive, there are other autoimmune conditions, or onset is in adulthood.
claims.source_text: [12.1] Intermittent HTG. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [12.2] Inconclusive genetic testing results. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 91.7%). [12.3] History of other autoimmune conditions. Strong expert consensus recommendation/statement (agreement: 83.3%). [12.4] Adult onset. … Autoimmune chylomicronemia can be caused by the presence of anti-GPIHBP1 antibodies.
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Use the same diagnostic approach** in patients admitted with acute pancreatitis, in pregnancy and in children (including those under 10).
claims.source_text: the diagnostic approach for FCS should not be changed under the following special circumstances: (a) patients hospitalized for acute pancreatitis; (b) pregnant patients; and (c) pediatric patients. … The diagnostic approach for patients aged under 10 years is comparable to that for adults
claims.locator: Latin American lipid and endocrine societies (Delphi panel), Archives of Endocrinology and Metabolism, 'A multi-society Delphi consensus statement on the diagnosis of familial chylomicronemia syndrome', 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12483350/, retrieved 2026-09-23
